comparator.name: Computer Science
comparator.route: Intelligent Interaction, High Performance Computing and the Year 3 elective semester with Project 3-1
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2025–2026 Education and Examination Regulations, Appendix 1 and Articles 3.15, 4.2 and 5.3 control this dated illustration. The course catalogue includes conflicting listings, so the example uses Object-Oriented Modelling and IT Management & Privacy as listed in the regulations and counts Operating Systems only in Year 3. The current programme page confirms the broad structure. This example uses the published 2025–2026 rules. Year 1 is twelve 4 EC courses and two 6 EC projects. Year 2 is ten 4 EC courses and two 10 EC modules with skills and project work. Year 3 is 24 EC of elective courses, a 6 EC project, three 4 EC core courses and an 18 EC thesis. The standard route assumes passing all preceding work on time. The thesis requires 138 EC overall, including all 60 first-year EC and at least 40 second-year EC.
components: Introduction to Computer Science (BCS1110, year 1 core course)
Objects in Programming (BCS1220, year 1 core course)
Data Structures and Algorithms (BCS1420, year 1 core course)
Introduction to Artificial Intelligence (BCS2120, year 2 core course)
Intelligent User Interfaces (BCS2130, year 2 core course)
Software Engineering and Architectures (BCS2210, year 2 core course)
Principles of Programming Languages (BCS2220, year 2 core course)
Project 3-1 (BCS3300, year 3 semester 1 project for external customers)
Year 3 electives (six 4 EC courses across Blocks 3.1 and 3.2)
Ethics and Philosophy for Computer Science
The individual thesis requires 138 EC overall, including all 60 first-year credits and at least 40 second-year credits.

routeSelection.route: Intelligent Interaction, High Performance Computing and the Year 3 elective semester with Project 3-1
routeSelection.basis: The generic Computer Science target permits one Year 2 module each semester. The first-listed module of each semester in the regulations and programme overview gives a neutral example. The Year 3 elective and project semester follows the regular in-programme route in Article 3.15.

core: Programming and software construction: procedural and object-oriented programming, object-oriented modelling, software engineering, programming languages and team software projects.
Algorithms and computation: data structures and algorithms, algorithmic design and the theory of computing, with algorithmic and computational thinking
Mathematical and logical foundations: discrete mathematics, logic, calculus, linear algebra, statistics and numerical methods
Computer systems: operating systems, networks, databases, computer security and parallel programming.
Research and project practice: project-centred learning in every semester and a bachelor's thesis carried out as an independent research project with a research plan
adjacent: Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, the AI and Machine Learning module, intelligent agents and learning from data

Intelligent interaction and robotics: human-computer interaction, Intelligent User Interfaces, image and video processing and robotics, with a laboratory for cognitive robotics and complex intelligent systems
Computing and society: computing ethics and philosophy, privacy and IT management, and the IT-Startups elective.
Specialised systems directions: high-performance computing, cybersecurity, embedded systems and quantum computing, together with the signals, control and numerical mathematics they rely on
Teaching computer science: an educational minor preparing students to teach computer science
questions: How can machines act intelligently, perceive their environment and interact with people?
How can reliable, complete software systems be designed and built in teams for real clients and for critical sectors such as healthcare and energy?
What can be computed at all, and how efficiently can it be computed?

trace: teaches structured and object-oriented programming in Python with testing and debugging, together with elements of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving; it directly implements the programming foundation of the core, which UM teaches in Procedural Programming and Objects in Programming
teaches differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations through projects; it directly implements the calculus foundation of the mathematical core

covers logic, discrete mathematics, patterns and structures with applications to computer science and algorithm construction; it directly implements the discrete-mathematics and logic strand of the core

teaches data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation with hands-on work and ends with an own research project analysing data; it makes a specific complementary contribution to data handling and empirical research practice, which the UM core does not teach as a separate course
teaches regression, classification, resampling, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering; it directly implements the machine-learning strand of the artificial-intelligence direction

has students build neural networks from scratch and in TensorFlow, apply them to vision and text and study large language models; it directly implements the deep-learning side of artificial intelligence and machine learning

teaches camera and image models, feature detection and the processing, analysis and understanding of image data with programming; it directly implements image and video processing, the course component of the Intelligent Interaction module

teaches planning and decision-making for AI systems in deterministic and non-deterministic environments with uncertainty and partial observability; it directly implements the agent-planning strand of artificial intelligence

teaches search, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction and optimisation by rational agents with weekly laboratory work; it directly implements the intelligent-agent and problem-solving methods of Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
Examines bias, interpretability, AI alignment and debates about the nature and moral status of intelligent machines.

teaches algorithm design and analysis, data structures and experimental performance analysis with laboratory work and larger algorithm projects; it directly implements the data structures and algorithms strand of the core

studies modern algebraic algorithms and solution methods for optimisation problems, with algorithmic thinking, mathematical modelling and experimental projects; it directly implements advanced algorithm design and analysis, although it does not cover the theory of computing
teaches systems of linear equations, matrices, vector spaces, linear independence, linear transformations and determinants; it directly implements the linear-algebra course of the core

characterises linear time-invariant systems through impulse and frequency response, convolution, Fourier representations and transfer functions; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the mathematics of signals and control behind UM's robotics and embedded-systems work, but UCR has no embedded-systems course
covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; it directly implements the probability and statistics course of the core

teaches numerical methods for root finding, differentiation and differential equations with attention to algorithm accuracy and sensitivity; it directly implements the numerical-methods course of the core
Develops multivariable and differential-equation methods for analysing computational models.
Connects Internet protocols and network architecture with operating-system resource management, processes and file systems.
teaches relational database management systems and SQL, relational database theory, normalisation and query processing; it directly implements the databases course of the core

teaches software development with C++ and Haskell and covers requirements gathering, software design, testing, quality assurance, deployment and maintenance with code reviews; it directly implements the software-engineering process and programming practice of the core
Develops venture concepts through customer validation, business modelling and a team pitch. This supports the business side of the IT-Startups direction.
Develops a strategic plan for responsible digital transformation and assesses organisational value and risks. The emphasis is business strategy.

teaches reinforcement-learning theory and algorithms and has students implement agents with neural networks that learn by trial and error; it directly implements learning agents in the artificial-intelligence direction

covers kinematics, manipulation, motion planning and computational problems of autonomous robots; it directly implements robotics, part of the intelligent systems and cognitive robotics that UM names among its applications

introduces functional brain anatomy, neural communication and the psychological and neuroscientific study of behaviour and cognition; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the foundation of the cognitive science behind cognitive robotics and human-computer interaction

explores the neural mechanisms of perception and action and how the brain processes sensory information to guide goal-directed behaviour; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the biological counterpart to machine perception and robotic action

treats higher-order cognitive processes including memory, attention, decision making and planning and trains experimental design; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the study of human decision making and planning that intelligent systems and interfaces are designed to support

asks what consciousness and mind are and whether large language models are or could be conscious; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the question whether machines can think, which UM raises in Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and The History and Philosophy of Computing

teaches virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism and practical ethics; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the ethical theory needed to analyse whether and how ethics can be designed into computer systems, a question named in The History and Philosophy of Computing
Designs experiments and fits and checks statistical models in R. It supports evaluating evidence in computational projects and in research on how people interact with technology.

alternatives.label: Computing, Mathematics and Data Science
alternatives.labelReason: Develop software, design and test algorithms, and study databases, networks and operating systems. Use mathematics and statistics to build and evaluate models in machine learning, computer vision and AI. Research methods and digital enterprise add practice in evaluating evidence and applying technology in organisations.
alternatives.concept: Develop software, design and test algorithms, and study databases, networks and operating systems. Use mathematics and statistics to build and evaluate models in machine learning, computer vision and AI. Research methods and digital enterprise add practice in evaluating evidence and applying technology in organisations.
progression: Programming precedes computer vision and algorithm design. Mathematical Methods precedes advanced mathematics and deep learning. The plan has four courses per semester and places Personal & Professional Development in Year 1.

alternatives.label: Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and Cognition
alternatives.labelReason: Study how machines learn, perceive and act. Combine machine learning, reinforcement learning, computer vision and robotics with the mathematics of signals and control. Study human perception and decision-making alongside questions about the ethics and philosophy of AI.
alternatives.concept: Study how machines learn, perceive and act. Combine machine learning, reinforcement learning, computer vision and robotics with the mathematics of signals and control. Study human perception and decision-making alongside questions about the ethics and philosophy of AI.
progression: Programming precedes computer vision and algorithm design. Mathematical Methods precedes advanced mathematics and deep learning. The plan has four courses per semester and places Personal & Professional Development in Year 1.
alternatives.distinctness: The AI option deepens machine learning with reinforcement learning and robotics, and pairs these methods with neuroscience, cognition and philosophy. The computing option instead develops software construction, networks and operating systems, databases, advanced algorithms, advanced calculus and digital enterprise. Each adds seven courses (52.5 EC) beyond the shared foundation.

characterises linear time-invariant systems through impulse and frequency response, convolution, Fourier representations and transfer functions; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the mathematics of signals and control used in robotics and perception

teaches numerical methods for root finding, differentiation and differential equations with attention to algorithm accuracy and sensitivity; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the numerical computation behind optimisation and the simulation of dynamical systems in learning and robotics

covers logic, discrete mathematics, patterns and structures with applications to computer science and algorithm construction; it directly implements the logical foundation of symbolic AI and decision-making

teaches algorithm design and analysis, data structures and experimental performance analysis; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the algorithmic foundation of search and learning methods

teaches structured and object-oriented programming in Python with testing and debugging; it directly implements the programming skills that every AI and machine-learning course in the programme requires
teaches matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations; it directly implements the linear-algebra foundation of machine learning and neural networks
covers probability theory, distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; it directly implements the probabilistic foundation of machine learning and decision-making under uncertainty
teaches differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations; it directly implements the calculus foundation needed for optimisation and neural-network training

examines AI fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility, the moral status of AI systems and the psychology of human-AI interaction; it directly implements the question of how intelligent machines relate to human agency and ethics
Designs experiments and fits and checks statistical models in R. It supports research on human decision-making and the evaluation of evidence about how people interact with technology.

candidates.label: Artificial intelligence, machine learning and intelligent interaction
Software for organisations and critical sectors, applied with business partners

selection.assessment: Two plans address substantial parts of the target. Computing, Mathematics and Data Science preserves the programming, algorithms, software, systems and mathematics core. Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and Cognition develops a distinct specialist direction. Each differs by seven courses (52.5 EC). Networks & Operating Systems and Linear Systems offer partial foundations for security and hardware applications. The workbook does not sustain dedicated progressions in computer security, parallel or high-performance computing, embedded programming, quantum computing or teaching computer science. Applied software for external clients shares the software, data and enterprise work of the computing option and lacks a separate sustained progression.

blocks: Both courses teach data types, control flow and procedures. UCR uses Python and Maastricht uses Java.
UCR builds programming and algorithmic skills across several courses. Maastricht combines an introductory survey with a microcontroller laboratory.
Introduction to Programming includes some object-oriented work. Maastricht offers a separate course covering classes, interfaces and polymorphism.
Both cover requirements, design, testing and maintenance. Maastricht also develops software architecture.
UCR uses C++ and Haskell for software development. Maastricht studies principles of programming languages in a separate course.
UCR covers object-oriented programming in its introductory Python course. Maastricht allocates a separate core course to object-oriented modelling.
Algorithms, logic and the theory of computing
Both teach algorithm design, data structures and performance analysis. The UCR course includes experimental performance analysis.
Both develop algorithmic design. UCR adds algebraic algorithms and optimisation. Maastricht covers greedy algorithms and dynamic programming.
Both develop discrete mathematical and logical tools for computing. Maastricht emphasises proof techniques.
UCR integrates logic into discrete mathematics. Maastricht teaches formal logic in a separate course.
Maastricht requires a separate course on computation and its theoretical limits.
Both develop differential and integral calculus. UCR also uses differential equations to build and analyse dynamic models.
Both teach systems of linear equations, matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.
Both cover probability, distributions and statistical inference. UCR uses computer algebra for simulation.
Both cover numerical methods for roots and differential equations. UCR examines accuracy and stability.
UCR covers networks and operating systems together, including Internet protocols. Maastricht assigns separate courses to networks and operating systems.
Operating systems are covered alongside networks in one UCR course. Maastricht gives operating systems a separate place in Year 3.
Both teach relational databases and SQL. UCR also covers normalisation and query processing.
UCR introduces concurrency in operating systems. Maastricht devotes a separate course to parallel programming.
UCR Robotics develops motion and manipulation. Maastricht’s embedded programming course focuses on programming devices.
Maastricht requires a dedicated computer security course.
Maastricht combines high-performance computing with a dedicated semester project.
Artificial intelligence, machine learning and robotics
Both study intelligent agents and methods for search and problem solving.
Both cover image processing. Maastricht combines the course with a semester project in human-computer interaction.
UCR studies human perception and the ethics of intelligent systems. Maastricht teaches the design and evaluation of intelligent interfaces.
Both examine ethical questions raised by computing. The UCR course focuses on AI.
UCR covers parts of this area through AI Ethics and Strategy & Digital Transformation. Maastricht requires a dedicated IT management and privacy course.
Research, project work, thesis and open electives
Maastricht gives credit for a semester-long team project. UCR embeds project work in individual courses.
Maastricht requires a second team project that draws on concurrent computing courses.
Maastricht offers a semester-long team project for an external client.
Six elective courses provide space to broaden or deepen study. The example leaves individual choices open.
Maastricht requires an 18 EC thesis. UCR’s 15 EC independent research option sits outside the scheduled course comparison.

notes.text: Maastricht requires specialist work in computer security, embedded programming, parallel computing, programming-language principles and theory of computation. The selected High Performance Computing module adds a semester project. UCR offers related foundations in software development, networks, operating systems, mathematics and AI.

Maastricht builds from a common computing core to specialist modules, team projects and an individual thesis. UCR’s two options use elective courses to develop different emphases in computing or AI. Optional UCR independent research is separate from the scheduled courses.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Computer Science bachelor combines programming, algorithms, mathematics and computer systems with team projects and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Maastricht example follows the published 2025–2026 regulations. Some course listings differ in the separate catalogue, and later years may change. UCR offers related study in software, algorithms and data, or in AI and robotics. Maastricht includes additional specialist computing and project work.
